title: Indexes
subtitle: Watch one query drop from reading 125,000 pages to a few dozen, then to three, and see what that speed costs on every write.
learn: How a B-tree index finds a row in a handful of page reads
Why the column order of a composite index decides which queries it can serve
How a covering index skips the table lookup entirely
Why every extra index slows down inserts, updates, and deletes
When the database correctly chooses a full scan over an index

steps.title: One query, ten million rows
steps.body: An orders table holds 10 million rows, about 100 bytes each, stored in 8 KB pages. That is roughly 1 GB across 125,000 pages. A user opens their order history, which runs: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42. The customer has about 50 orders. How should the database find those 50 rows?
steps.idea: Finding a few rows among millions is the problem an index exists to solve.
steps.caption: A query arrives for one customer's orders.

steps.title: Without an index: read everything
steps.body: With no index on customer_id, the engine must read every page of the table and test every row. Pages pass through the buffer pool, the database's RAM cache of recently used pages. That is 125,000 pages and 10 million row checks to return 50 rows. Sequential reads are fast, but about 1 GB of work still takes on the order of a second, and it grows linearly with the table.
steps.idea: A full scan costs time proportional to table size, no matter how few rows match.
steps.caption: Every table page is read to find 50 rows.

steps.title: A B-tree is a sorted map of pages
steps.body: An index is a separate structure holding the indexed column's values in sorted order, each with a pointer to its table row. Most databases use a B-tree (strictly a B+tree: data pointers live only in the leaves): a shallow tree where each page holds hundreds of keys. Internal pages guide you down, and leaf pages hold the entries in order. Leaf pages are linked in sorted order, so a range or ORDER BY just walks along the leaves. With about 300 keys per page, three levels cover roughly 27 million entries.
steps.idea: A wide, shallow tree means any key is only a few page reads away, even in a huge table.
steps.caption: The index is a small sorted structure beside the table.

steps.title: With an index: seek, then fetch
steps.body: Now the engine walks the tree: root page, one internal page, then a leaf page, which lists the 50 entries for customer 42 side by side. For each entry it follows the pointer to the table page holding the full row. Upper levels are hot and stay in RAM, so the cost is about 3 index pages plus up to one table page per row. Here that is roughly 53 pages instead of 125,000.
steps.idea: An index seek reads a handful of pages instead of the whole table; cost grows with tree depth, not table size.
steps.caption: Tree walk to the leaf, then fetch matching rows.

steps.title: Column order in a composite index
steps.body: The page needs the latest 20 orders (WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20), so you create an index on (customer_id, created_at). Entries are sorted by customer_id, then created_at within each customer. The engine jumps to customer 42's block, already in date order, and reads the last 20 entries with no separate sort. A query filtering only on created_at cannot seek into it, because dates are scattered across all customers. This is the leftmost-prefix rule.
steps.idea: A composite index serves queries that use its leading columns; put equality columns first, then the range or sort column.
steps.caption: Entries sorted by customer, then date: 20 rows read.

steps.title: Covering index: skip the table
steps.body: Suppose the page only shows order date and total. If the index also stores total (for example (customer_id, created_at) INCLUDE (total), or the equivalent in your database), the leaf entries already hold every column the query needs. The engine answers from the index alone, skipping the scattered row fetches that are often the most expensive part of a seek. (In PostgreSQL this relies on VACUUM keeping the visibility map current; otherwise some table visits remain.)
steps.idea: A covering index answers a query entirely from the index, trading a larger index for fewer reads.
steps.caption: The index alone answers the query.

steps.title: Every index taxes every write
steps.body: Now an order is inserted. The row goes into a table page, and a matching entry must go into each index, in its sorted position. With five indexes that is six places to write, and a full leaf page may split in two, touching its parent as well. The 6 shown are pages written, not counting the tree walks (reads) needed to locate each position. Updates to indexed columns move entries, and deletes remove them. Indexes buy read speed with write cost.
steps.idea: Write cost grows with the number of indexes, so add them for real query patterns, not by habit.
steps.caption: One insert updates the table and five indexes.

steps.title: When a scan is the right answer
steps.body: Suppose a query asks for orders with status = 'shipped', and 90 percent of rows match. Following the index would mean 9 million random row fetches, far worse than reading the table once in order. The query planner estimates this from statistics and chooses the full scan. A scan can also be forced when the index cannot be used: wrapping a column in a function, such as WHERE lower(email) = ..., usually bypasses a plain index on email, and an expression index on lower(email) fixes that.
steps.idea: Indexes help selective queries; when most rows match, a sequential scan is cheaper and the planner knows it.
steps.caption: Index skipped: the scan is cheaper for 90 percent of rows.

steps.title: Index for the queries you run
steps.body: A B-tree turns a search over millions of rows into a few page reads. Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule, so column order matters. Covering indexes skip the table. Each index slows writes and uses space, and queries that match most of the table are better served by scans. Look at real slow queries and their query plans, then add the smallest index that fixes them.
steps.idea: Design indexes from your actual queries, check the query plan, and keep only the ones that earn their write cost.
steps.caption: Fast reads, paid for on every write.

quiz.q: A table has an index on (customer_id, created_at). Which query can use it most effectively?
quiz.why: The index is sorted by customer_id first, so a query with an equality on customer_id lets the engine jump to one block, then range over created_at inside it. A filter on created_at alone skips the leading column.

quiz.q: Your table grows from 10 million to 100 million rows. How does a B-tree seek on a single key change?
options: It stays almost the same, maybe one extra level
quiz.why: B-trees are wide and shallow, so a tenfold growth adds at most about one level. A full scan, by contrast, would take roughly ten times longer.

quiz.q: A write-heavy table has 12 indexes, and inserts have become slow. What is the most sensible first step?
options: Find indexes no query plan uses and drop them
Add more RAM to the server
Convert every index into a covering index
Make the existing indexes covering by adding every column
quiz.why: Each insert updates all 12 indexes. Removing unused or redundant ones cuts write cost without hurting reads. Covering indexes would make each index larger and slower to maintain.

quiz.q: A query matches 80 percent of a table and the planner ignores the index. What is the likely explanation?
options: Indexes only work on unique columns
A sequential scan is cheaper than millions of random row fetches
quiz.why: Following an index means one random table lookup per match. When most rows qualify, reading the table once in order is cheaper, and the planner picks that using its statistics.

cheatsheet.def: Sorted, shallow tree of pages mapping key values to row locations. Good for equality, ranges, and ordering. Seek cost grows with depth, not table size.
A scan reads every page and costs O(table size). A seek walks the tree to matching entries and costs a few page reads plus any row fetches.

A composite index on (a, b, c) serves filters on a, on a and b, or on a, b and c, but a filter on b or c alone cannot seek into it (some engines can skip-scan, which only pays off when the leading column has few distinct values).
Put equality-filtered columns first, then the range or sort column. Selectivity and your real queries break ties.
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the table is never read. Costs a bigger index and more write work.
Every insert adds an entry to every index. Updates to indexed columns and deletes also maintain the affected indexes. Page splits add more work, and more indexes means slower writes and more storage.
How few rows a filter keeps. A filter that keeps 50 of 10 million rows is highly selective and benefits from an index; one that keeps 90 percent is not selective, and a scan wins.
The engine's chosen strategy for a query. Check it (EXPLAIN) to confirm an index is used instead of guessing.
